 Updated: 5:56 PM EST Nov 20, 2026 Editorial Standards ⓘ Jessica Brown Anchor/Reporter BOSTON — The Korean beauty trend known as "glass skin" is gaining popularity in the U.S., offering glowing, hydrated skin through innovative products and treatments. 
 "Glass skin is essentially like skin that is translucent," said Beth Gillette , beauty editor at Cosmopolitan. "It can come from products, it can come from treatments. But it's really just the idea of really glowy, hydrated skin. And that is the goal of K-beauty." 
 Advertisement South Korea has become a major player in the global cosmetics market, ranking second only to France in exports. 
 Some Americans even travel to Seoul to explore the products firsthand. 
 "A lot of my routine is Korean skincare actually," said Gillette, who has visited South Korea twice. "The thing I come home with every time is sunscreen. They're lighter weight. They feel better on your skin." 
 Dr. Farah Moustafa , a dermatologist at Tufts Medical Center, emphasized the significance of sunscreen in K-beauty routines. 
 "They take it very seriously," she said. "A lot of the viral products are sunscreen products, and a lot of people seek out Korean skincare specifically for their UV filters that we can't access here in the U.S."
 Moustafa carries a K-beauty sunscreen that she bought locally in her makeup bag. 
 "It's using our UV filters ," she said. "If you got this product in Korea, you get it with their UV filters. It's still a nice lightweight formula and I like it a lot. People go specifically to get their sunscreen from there because the UV filters are just so great." 
 Other K-beauty products gaining attention include snail mucin, which Moustafa said is "very well tolerated and very hydrating."
 She also uses a lip balm containing propolis, a substance collected by honeybees. 
 "I have to say, this is one of the nicer lip products that I've ever used," Moustafa said. "It's anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial. So the idea is that you're putting something kind of soothing on the skin."
 One ingredient Moustafa remains cautious about is PDRN , which is derived from salmon sperm. 
 "The idea is that, when applied topically or when injected, these are kind of stimulating collagen production," she said. "I would want to see more like real randomized controlled trials, real evidence for use in this case before I would feel really comfortable with that product."
 Gillette highlighted the appeal of K-beauty staples like sheet masks, toner pads, and under-eye patches.
 "They kind of embrace the glow, the dew, what we might think of as shine," she said. "They love it. That's what they want."
